Export as

C3D is written as a binary point-data file with the marker labels preserved. FBX is written as ASCII with one animated node per marker — readable by Motive, MotionBuilder, Maya and Blender, though it carries markers only, not a solved skeleton. TRC is the OpenSim/Mocap plain-text marker format.

Using this tool

  • Gait: load a file — .c3d (Motive/OptiTrack or Captury), .bvh (Captury), or .csv (Captury — angle/clinical-metric data only, not enough position data for 3D rendering). OptiTrack C3D: pick the subject, then click "Analyse gait" for the full report. Captury BVH/C3D: loads straight into the 3D viewer; click "Analyse gait" there for stride timing and joint angles.
  • Golf: load a .c3d file with body + club rigid-body markers. If multiple people are in the file, the active swinger is auto-identified by club speed but always shown so you can check it's right.
  • Bike Fit: load a .c3d file with a pedalling trial. A steady-cadence section is auto-detected within the file — no need to trim the recording yourself.
  • Multiple people in a file: any protocol will show a participant picker if it finds more than one plausible person (based on marker count) — the auto-pick is a starting point, always overridable.
  • 3D viewer (same across all three protocols): drag to orbit, right-click or shift+drag to pan, scroll to zoom. Toggle Markers/Sticks/Skeleton independently. With Skeleton on, click a bone to identify it. The dashed line on every chart tracks the viewer's current frame — play or scrub to see it move.
  • Notes: add a text note at the current frame to flag something for later — shows as a tick on the scrub bar and in the list below it.
  • Print / Save as PDF: each protocol's report has its own button, top-left of the results.

Start here

The animation pipeline — how the four tools connect

The Animation tools are meant to be used in sequence, and hand work to each other without re-picking the file: File Review → Data Cleaning → ReTargeting → File Export, and File Export can send straight back to File Review so you can check a result before delivering it.

Each tool has "Send to …" buttons for the steps that make sense from where you are. The handover keeps the marker data in memory only — a take is tens of megabytes of float data, far past what browser storage can hold, which is the same reason session history keeps summaries rather than the capture itself. Reloading the page clears it.

You don't have to use every step. Review then Export is fine if the data is already clean; Cleaning then Export skips retargeting entirely.

Architecture note

This tool runs entirely client-side — a single HTML file, no server, nothing leaves your browser.

OpenSim and pyCGM2 are both real, widely-used biomechanics packages — but OpenSim is C++/Python and pyCGM2 is Python, and neither can run inside a browser. So neither is a dependency here: everything below is a custom, from-scratch JavaScript implementation, built to follow a specific named published method where one exists, and clearly flagged as our own approximation where the marker set or browser-only environment doesn't support the fully rigorous version. This page exists so that's always clear, rather than something you'd have to ask about.

Libraries & tools this depends on

The complete list — nothing else is loaded, and there's no server-side component or external API call anywhere in this tool.

  • Chart.js 4.4.1 (chartjs.org) — every 2D chart (joint angles, phase portraits, whole-trial/whole-file/whole-ride views). Embedded directly in this file.
  • three.js r128 (threejs.org) — the 3D skeleton viewer for every protocol. Embedded directly in this file. Note: r128 specifically — some APIs used here (e.g. no OrbitControls import, custom orbit/pan/zoom instead) don't carry over cleanly to newer versions.
  • Everything else — C3D/BVH parsing, all biomechanics calculations, the 3D rendering logic itself, PDF/print layout — is custom code in this file. No parsing library, no physics engine, no analytics, no fonts or assets fetched from anywhere else.

Both libraries are embedded directly in this HTML file (not fetched from a CDN), so the whole page works with no internet access at all — needed for the Live Capture tab, which is typically used on a closed studio network with no internet available.

Running it locally & reusing the code

Download Tool in the footer gives you everything needed to run this yourself: the page itself, the two Live Capture bridge scripts, the extended Captury binding with its build notes, and a README. Your browser may ask permission for multiple downloads — that's expected, they arrive as separate files rather than a zip.

The app is one self-contained HTML file: open it directly, or serve the folder (npx serve .) if local file restrictions get in the way. To host it, drop the single file on Netlify or any static host. The bridge scripts run on your own machine, separately from the page.

The README covers lifting individual functions into your own project — worth reading the architecture note below first, since the two coordinate spaces and the FBX loader patches are the traps someone extracting code without that context would hit.

Live Capture

OptiTrack (Motive) Live Capture setup

Written so this can be followed fully offline once on the studio network. Applies specifically to OptiTrack/Motive — see the Captury note further down.

What you need:

  • A laptop that can join the studio's closed WiFi/Ethernet network (the one broadcasting from the Motive machine's IP). This does NOT need to be the Motive machine itself — any device on the same network/multicast segment works, since NatNet is UDP multicast, not a direct connection to Motive.
  • Python 3 on that laptop, with two packages installed. Windows: py -m pip install natnet websockets. Mac/Linux: python3 -m pip install natnet websockets (add --break-system-packages if pip complains about an externally-managed environment). Using -m pip rather than a bare pip makes sure the packages land in the same Python you'll run the bridge with, which is the usual cause of "it's installed but the script says it isn't".
  • natnet_bridge.py — use the download button above; it's embedded directly in this page, so it's available wherever this tool is hosted, not just from wherever you originally received it.
  • This HTML file, opened in a browser on that same laptop.

Step 1 — find your laptop's IP on the studio network. Once connected (and disconnected from the internet, if that's the setup): Windows — Command Prompt, run ipconfig, look for the IPv4 address under the active adapter. Mac — System Settings → Network → the active connection → the IP address shown. Linux — ip addr or hostname -I. You need an address on the same subnet as the Motive machine — if your laptop shows something completely different, it likely hasn't picked up an address on that network yet.

Step 2 — run the bridge:

Windows: py natnet_bridge.py --server-ip <motive-ip> --local-ip <your-laptop-ip> Mac/Linux: python3 natnet_bridge.py --server-ip <motive-ip> --local-ip <your-laptop-ip>

On Windows, there is no python3 command — that name only exists on Mac and Linux. Use py (the launcher installed with Python from python.org) or python. Two traps worth knowing: typing python3 on Windows often opens the Microsoft Store instead of an error, because Windows ships a Store shortcut under that name — that is not Python and the bridge will never start from it (turn it off under Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases). And if python reports "not recognised", Python either isn't installed or wasn't added to PATH — the python.org installer has an Add python.exe to PATH checkbox on the first screen that is easy to miss; re-running the installer and choosing Modify can add it without a reinstall.

If you get WinError 10049 — The requested address is not valid in its context: that is a bug in the natnet package on Windows, not your setup. In multicast mode it binds its data socket to the multicast group address itself, which Linux and macOS allow but Windows forbids — a socket there may only bind to a real local address or to all of them. The bridge now patches this at startup (binding all interfaces and joining the group instead, which is the portable form) and logs that it has done so, so an up-to-date natnet_bridge.py from the button above should not hit it. The library's own error text blames Motive's multicast/unicast setting, which sends you looking in the wrong place.

Other causes of the same error: a --local-ip that isn't actually one of this machine's addresses. The bridge now checks this at startup and prints the addresses it did find. If Motive is set to Unicast rather than Multicast in its Data Streaming pane, add --unicast — the two ends must agree.

Replace both placeholders with the real addresses — don't type the angle brackets literally. You should see a "Connected to Motive" message and a WebSocket server listening on ws://0.0.0.0:8765. A few "Connect attempt X/5 timed out, retrying..." lines before connecting is expected and fine — the bridge retries automatically since the underlying protocol only sends one connection request per attempt. If all 5 attempts fail, check that Motive is actually streaming (Data Streaming pane, "Broadcast Frame Data" on), that --server-ip matches the Motive machine, that your laptop's --local-ip is genuinely on the same network segment, and that no firewall is blocking inbound UDP on ports 1510/1511.

Step 3 — connect the browser app. Open this file in a browser on the same laptop the bridge is running on, go to the Live Capture tab, and click Connect (the WebSocket address defaults to ws://localhost:8765, correct when the browser and bridge are on the same machine). You should see the connection status change to "Connected" and a list of detected marker sets / rigid bodies / skeletons appear.

Step 4 — record and analyse. Click Start recording when ready, Stop recording when done, then Analyse as gait trial — this sends the whole recording straight into the same analysis pipeline used for a loaded C3D file. No file needs to be saved or reloaded.

Optional — accessing this remotely (e.g. from a different network). If the Motive machine has internet access, pair the bridge with a token so the stream isn't open to anyone who finds the address:

Windows: py natnet_bridge.py --server-ip 127.0.0.1 --local-ip 127.0.0.1 --auth-token my-secret-here Mac/Linux: python3 natnet_bridge.py --server-ip 127.0.0.1 --local-ip 127.0.0.1 --auth-token my-secret-here

(Run the bridge on the Motive machine itself in this case.) Then start a tunnel in a separate terminal (e.g. ngrok http 8765 or a Cloudflare Tunnel) to get a public wss:// address, and enter that plus the token in the Live Capture tab. Without --auth-token, the bridge accepts any connection — fine for a closed local network, not recommended once reachable from the open internet.

This pipeline was built and tested against a mock Motive server, since real studio hardware isn't reachable from here — that caught and fixed three real bugs (a missing protocol field, a version mismatch, and a connection-retry gap), so the wire protocol handling is validated. What can't be verified from here is the real Motive machine's exact behaviour in this specific setup (protocol version, marker naming, network quirks). If something doesn't connect or marker names look unexpected, that's the most likely place to check first — not a fundamental protocol issue.

Captury

File-based import (BVH/C3D) and live streaming are both supported.

File-based (fully tested): export a recording from Captury Live or Captury Studio as BVH or C3D, then load that file directly in the Captury tab here — same as any other file. BVH carries the full skeleton hierarchy (69 bones in a typical export, including fingers); C3D carries a reduced marker/joint set (22 in the validated sample). Both were tested end-to-end against real Captury export files, including the marker-visibility tree, trail/overlay dropdowns, and the gait analysis pipeline.

Live streaming: built directly from Captury's own public source (github.com/thecaptury/RemoteCaptury), not from guesswork. Uses their official, pip-installable remotecaptury package for the connection and pose stream, plus one small addition — the stock package doesn't expose joint names at all, so an extended build adds that one missing piece (a few lines wrapping their own existing Captury_getActor() C++ function). Without the extended build, streaming still works, just with generic unlabelled dots instead of a connected skeleton.

Setup: install the packages with py -m pip install remotecaptury websockets on Windows or python3 -m pip install remotecaptury websockets on Mac/Linux, then run py captury_bridge.py --server-ip <captury-live-machine-ip> (Windows) or python3 captury_bridge.py --server-ip <captury-live-machine-ip> (Mac/Linux) on a laptop on the same network as CapturyLive — same shape as the OptiTrack setup above. For named joints and a rendered skeleton (rather than plain dots), download all three files above and follow the build guide — it needs a C++ compiler, the same one required to build the stock package in the first place.

Validated by writing a mock CapturyLive server directly from the real protocol in RemoteCaptury.cpp — not by inventing one — and testing the bridge against it using Captury's actual, official client library, end to end: skeleton definition, joint-to-name resolution, and the live pose stream all confirmed flowing correctly through to the browser. That process caught and fixed two real protocol bugs (the pose stream needs a specific source port to reach the client at all, and bone types arrive via a separate packet the first version missed). What's not verified: real CapturyLive hardware behaviour, specifically units (assumed millimetres, per --units) and which axis is "up" (assumed Z, per --up-axis) — both are guesses documented as such, with CLI flags to correct them once you can check against a real skeleton. If the skeleton renders at roughly 1000x the expected size or lying on its side, that's the first thing to flip.

Biomechanics protocols

Gait event detection (heel-strike / toe-off)

Zeni, J.A., Richards, J.G., Higginson, J.S. (2008). "Two simple methods for determining gait events during treadmill and overground walking using kinematic data." Gait & Posture, 27(4), 710-714.

  • Directly follows the paper's core method: anteroposterior distance between heel/toe markers and the pelvis centroid, with heel-strike as a local maximum and toe-off as a local minimum.
  • The smoothing window (8% of stride length) is our own tuning choice, not specified by the paper.
Joint angles (pelvis tilt/obliquity/rotation; hip/knee/ankle flexion)
  • Follows the same general idea used across clinical gait systems (Vicon Plug-in Gait / Conventional Gait Model, OpenSim's gait2392, and similar) — decomposing one segment's orientation relative to another, or to a lab reference for the pelvis, into three rotation components. This is our own implementation of that general idea, not a port of any specific system's code, axis order, or sign convention.
  • Decomposition uses three.js's own rotation-matrix-to-Euler conversion; the axis order and signs were chosen and validated against expected clinical ranges (documented directly in the code), not copied from a specific paper's exact sequence.
  • Segment coordinate systems use whatever markers are actually available: full ASIS/PSIS-based anatomical axes for the pelvis, but no bilateral condyle/malleolus markers for thigh/shank, so those use an approximation via "wand" markers instead — a genuine limitation, not a rigorous joint coordinate system.
Hip & shoulder joint centre estimation (HJC / SJC)
  • Not a specific published regression (e.g. Bell et al. 1990, Harrington et al. 2007) — an earlier Bell-style implementation was replaced with a simpler ASIS/PSIS-midpoint method after finding it worked better for this marker set.
  • The shoulder joint centre offset (medial + inferior from the acromion marker) is a hand-tuned approximation refined through iterative visual feedback, not a cited formula.
  • Anatomically motivated, but not a rigorous regression — worth knowing if precise HJC/SJC accuracy matters for your use case.
Anthropometric plausibility check

Drillis, R., & Contini, R. (1966). "Body segment parameters." New York University, School of Engineering and Science.

  • Segment-length-to-height ratios used to flag implausible marker-derived measurements.
  • Several ratios were recalibrated specifically for this marker set, since its exact landmarks differ from the original paper's definitions — treat these as close to the published ratios, not exact matches.
Golf: kinematic sequence & X-factor

McTeigue, M., Lamb, S.R., Mottram, R., Pirozzolo, F. (1994). "Spine and hip motion analysis during the golf swing." Science and Golf II. Cheetham, P.J. et al. (2008). "The importance of stretching the 'X-Factor' in the downswing of golf: A biomechanical review." Science and Golf and related work associated with groups like TPI.

  • Follows the same general "summation of speed" principle these describe — pelvis, then shoulders, then club, each peaking later and faster than the last in an efficient swing — and the X-factor concept (hip-shoulder rotational separation). This is our own implementation of those ideas, not a port of any specific system's algorithm.
  • Pelvis/shoulder rotation is tracked as the angle of a marker-to-marker line (hip-to-hip, shoulder-to-shoulder) projected onto the horizontal plane — a genuine simplification, not a full 3D segment coordinate system. A golf swing involves substantial spine tilt and lateral bend, which this projection doesn't account for — likely why the X-factor this produces reads higher than commonly-published values (typically 40-50° for skilled golfers). Treat as a first-pass estimate.
  • The swing window (address / top of backswing / impact / follow-through) is detected automatically from club speed, by finding the fastest clean swing in the file and searching outward for sustained stillness on each side — a heuristic, not a validated phase-detection algorithm. If a file has multiple swings, this picks whichever one has the highest peak club speed.
  • When multiple people appear in a file (e.g. a golfer and a caddie), the active swinger is identified by matching each body to its own club by name similarity, then comparing peak club speed between candidates — not by any assumption about names or roles.
Bike fit: crank position, knee tracking & pelvic stability
  • Standard convention from the general cycling-biomechanics literature — joint angles at the three classic crank reference positions (top of stroke, bottom of stroke, "3 o'clock" during the power phase) — not a specific commercial fit system's exact method.
  • Crank angle isn't measured directly (no crank-angle sensor in a marker-based capture) — it's inferred from the ankle's own roughly-circular path during pedalling. Which plane that circle lies in is checked per file rather than assumed (verified directly: it is NOT the same "forward" axis convention gait analysis uses for this capture — the true pedalling plane had to be found by checking the data, not assumed from another protocol's convention).
  • "3 o'clock" specifically is approximated as 25% of the way (by time) from top of stroke to the next top, assuming roughly constant angular velocity within one cycle — a reasonable approximation for steady pedalling, verified directly against the true crank-angle calculation for a real steady-cadence sample, not a physical measurement.
  • Knee tracking is the same knee ab/adduction (valgus[+]/varus[-]) calculation used for gait, centred on this ride's own mean for the same reason gait's is (see the joint angles note above) — not compared against a published "safe" range, since no such citation is used here.
  • Each side's joint angles are evaluated at its own cycle's key positions, not both sides evaluated against one side's timing — worth naming directly because getting this wrong (comparing left at right's "top of stroke", when the two legs are naturally ~180° out of phase) produces convincing-looking but meaningless 60-120% "asymmetry" numbers, which is exactly what an earlier version of this tool did before being corrected.
  • Torso lean is the angle between the trunk's long axis (pelvis-to-shoulder line) and true vertical — a single-angle simplification, not a full spinal posture analysis.
"Observations" panels

Each report includes an Observations panel — asymmetries between left and right, or values outside a commonly-cited range, computed directly from that trial's own numbers. These are not a diagnosis or clinical judgement. This tool has no way to know whether a given number reflects a genuine issue for a specific person — only whether it's unusual relative to that person's own other side, or a published range cited elsewhere on this page. Thresholds (e.g. flagging an asymmetry over a given percentage) are our own choices for what's worth surfacing, not a clinical cutoff from any source.

What this means practically

If you need results directly comparable to a specific commercial system's exact numbers — Vicon Plug-in Gait, STT's 3DMA, OpenSim — this tool's absolute values won't necessarily match. The methods are inspired by the same general biomechanical conventions, but weren't cross-validated against those specific systems.

Animation tools

File Review — annotations, timecode & export

Loads any playable format (OptiTrack or Captury C3D, Captury BVH, FBX) purely for scrubbing and note-taking, with no protocol-specific analysis attached. Drop a note at the current frame and every note is tagged with frame number, elapsed seconds, and embedded timecode where the file carries one.

Timecode: OptiTrack C3D exports carry a genuine SMPTE start timecode (HH:MM:SS:FF) in the file's TIMECODE parameter group, along with its standard (NTSC / PAL / FILM) and drop-frame flag. That timecode clock is independent of the mocap capture rate — a 120 Hz capture synced to 30 fps timecode is normal. Where a file has no timecode group (many analog/force-plate trials don't), notes fall back to frame and seconds only rather than inventing a timecode.

Drop-frame timecode's periodic frame-number skipping is not applied, so on drop-frame material the value can drift by up to a couple of frames per minute. That's flagged with an asterisk on the timecode. Fine for review and reference; not frame-accurate for broadcast conform.

Export: CSV (frame, seconds, timecode, note — RFC 4180 quoted, so commas and quotes in your notes survive) or plain text for pasting into a ticket or email.

Data Cleaning — what the automatic detection can and can't do

The flagged list is a ranked review queue, worst first, not a verdict. It was measured against real raw/cleaned FBX pairs by asking: does it surface the markers a professional cleaner actually corrected? Across both test files, it missed none of them — every marker that received a substantial correction appeared in the list. On the file with real work to do, the top ten were all genuinely broken; on a file that was already nearly clean, the one marker needing attention ranked inside the top ten of a hundred-plus.

So treat it as a screen that reliably puts the real problems near the top, and expect the tail of the list to contain markers that are fine. It is deliberately tuned that way round: missing a broken marker costs you a re-delivery, while an extra name on a short list costs you a glance.

Pick the subject you're reviewing when a take has more than one. Rigidity is judged within each subject, but a prop ranks on the same list — a dribbled ball's markers occlude constantly and genuinely do break rigidity, and on the basketball trial used for testing they filled the top three places ahead of the performer. Filtering to the performer is what turns the top ten from a fifth correct into entirely correct.

What it can't see: occlusion. A capture system knows which markers were reconstructed rather than actually seen, and that confidence data is not written into an exported FBX — by the time data is FBX the trajectories are already continuous, with no gaps or dropouts left to find (confirmed on raw, pre-cleanup exports: zero missing or non-finite frames). A geometry-only check therefore can't reproduce every decision a cleaner makes with the original capture in front of them. C3D preserves more of this than FBX does.

The repair, filter and swap operations are deterministic and verified separately: an injected pop was detected and repaired to zero residual error, the Butterworth filter cut high-frequency noise by ~260x while leaving peak timing on exactly the same frame (zero-lag), and swaps exchange precisely the frames asked for.

Data Cleaning — repair, filter and swap (what each one does)

Repair interpolates across flagged frames from the good frames either side, rather than deleting them — a continuous trajectory is easier for everything downstream than a hole. A gap at the very start or end holds the nearest good value instead, since there's nothing to interpolate between.

Butterworth low-pass is the standard biomechanics filter, run forwards then backwards so it adds no phase lag. That matters: a filter that shifts the signal moves the very event times (heel strike, peak speed) you're trying to measure. Verified on synthetic data — high-frequency noise dropped ~260x while a known peak stayed on exactly the same frame. 6 Hz is the usual starting point for human movement; raise it if you're losing genuine fast detail, lower it if noise persists. Moving average is the blunter alternative.

Swap range exchanges two markers' positions over a frame range, for when the system has labelled a pair the wrong way round. It does exactly what you ask over exactly the frames you give it — no detection involved.

Every operation is undoable, and "Reset to original" returns to the file as loaded. Applying a filter or repair invalidates the current analysis, so re-run Analyse to see what remains.

ReTargeting — scope, validation and limits

Validated against 13 real rigs (v5.8.1), not yet against the standalone tool's own output. Loading and characterization now check out on real Mixamo/Unreal/MetaHuman-class FBX rigs from 64 to 6,561 bones, plus BVH — four real bugs found this way are fixed (see HANDOVER.md §"v5.8.1 — real-file validation findings"). The topology characterizer is still a practical reimplementation of the standalone tool's approach, not a line-for-line port of its 1,300-line original, and no side-by-side screenshot check against the standalone app's own verdicts has been done yet. Needs a close-to-neutral bind pose to be reliable — animation-take exports that bake a mid-motion frame as their "rest" transform (confirmed on a yoga pose and a dance capture) will show low confidence or inflated rest-pose divergence; the verdict box below explains when that's happening. Dense character rigs with extensive facial/cloth bones can still over-count limb pairs. See the Help tab for the full portability notes.

Portable, and built here: loading two skeletons and pairing their bones, the colour-coded verdict (will renaming alone work, or not, and why), hip-height scale ratio, per-bone mapping status with manual override, and the mapping exports (bonemap.csv / .json / report). All of that is geometry and string matching — no external dependency.

Not portable, and won't be: the retarget bake. RigMatch does that through Blender running headless (mar_retarget.py, using Blender's own bpy and armature evaluation). A browser page can't run Blender, so baking a delivered FBX stays a job for the standalone tool or a Blender step. The same goes for its Unreal asset writing, and for Simulate/Write FBX playback.

Comparison view is a 2D schematic, not the 3D orbit viewer. Wiring two more instances of this app's WebGL viewer couldn't be visually verified while building it (no browser available), so this ships a simpler front-view projection instead of a feature that was never actually seen rendering correctly.

ReTargeting — how the motion transfer actually works

What gets copied is each bone's rotation away from its own bind pose, not its absolute orientation. That's what lets a T-posed mocap rig drive an A-posed character: copying absolute orientations only works when both rigs happen to share a bind pose, which in practice they rarely do.

Verified directly: a T-posed source at rest leaves an A-posed target at its own rest pose (zero error), and a 90° elbow bend arrives as exactly 90° on the differently-posed rig. Retargeting a rig onto itself reproduces the original motion exactly.

Root motion is scaled by the height ratio between the rigs, so a shorter character takes proportionally shorter strides instead of skating or over-striding. You can switch this off if you want the motion copied in absolute units.

Bone lengths are never changed — only roots translate, every other bone keeps its bind offset, so the target keeps its own proportions rather than being stretched to match the source. Measured drift across a real take: about 1e-13 units.

The bone mapping is the weak link, not the transfer. The bake faithfully does whatever the mapping says, so a mis-paired bone gives wrong motion. Check the mapping table before baking, and use the per-bone override dropdown where it's wrong — overrides are respected by the bake.

Export formats — what each one carries, and what's verified

C3D (File Export) — binary point data with marker labels, frame rate and units preserved. Verified by writing a file and reading it back with this app's own C3D parser: labels, rate and frame count all survive, coordinates to float precision.

Skeletal FBX (ReTargeting) — a real bone hierarchy with per-bone rotation curves and root translation curves. Verified by round trip on real data: retarget a Motive take onto a Mixamo rig, export, re-import, compare joint positions frame by frame — max error 3.3e-5 across 221 bones. Rotation order was pinned by measuring every option rather than reading the spec, since that's where FBX exporters usually go quietly wrong.

BVH (ReTargeting) — skeleton plus motion as plain text, read by MotionBuilder, Maya, Blender and Unreal without a plugin. Round-trips through this app's own BVH reader.

FBX (ASCII) in File Export carries markers only, not a solved skeleton — use ReTargeting's skeletal FBX if you need bones. TRC is the OpenSim marker format; CSV is one row per frame, for spreadsheets and scripts.

Duplicate bone names are renamed on export. Rigs genuinely ship with repeats — the Mixamo Y-Bot has four nodes called mixamorigHips — and a file with repeated node names is ambiguous to every importer; re-importing one matched the wrong bones and threw positions out by metres. Later duplicates get a numeric suffix; the first keeps its original name.

Worth one check before a client delivery: the FBX round trip is verified against this app's importer. FBX rotation-order semantics differ between packages, so confirm one export in MotionBuilder or Maya before relying on it.

File formats & rigs

FBX units, scale & world space

FBX files declare their own unit scale, and different exporters disagree. The relevant field is GlobalSettings.UnitScaleFactor, expressed in centimetres per file unit: 0.1 means a millimetre file, 1 means centimetres, 100 means metres. This tool reads that field and converts to metres, rather than assuming a unit.

That matters more than it sounds. Of three real sample files tested here, one declared millimetres and two declared centimetres — an assumed-millimetre reading made the latter two come in 10× too small. If a person-sized subject reads as 0.2 m or 20 m, the unit is being read wrongly and the Scale override (Auto / mm / cm / m) will fix it.

Up axis: read from the file's UpAxis setting and converted to this tool's Z-up convention. Y-up is the FBX norm. Override if a file is authored unusually and the subject appears lying on its side.

Ground & centre on origin: places the lowest point of the take on the floor and centres travel about the origin, so a subject authored far from the origin still appears on the grid. Measured across the whole take, not one frame — grounding on a single frame plants the subject correctly for that instant but sinks or floats them through a jump, crouch or lunge.

FBX animation layers

An FBX take can hold several animation layers — a base take plus corrective layers on top. Retargeted files commonly do; one sample here carries a second layer literally named SpineAdjustment affecting the spine and both shoulders.

Each layer is exposed as its own selectable clip, so you can inspect what a corrective layer contains. Layers the file marks as empty are listed but disabled, so you can see they exist without chasing nothing.

Layers are shown one at a time, not combined. How FBX layers blend is governed by BlendMode and Weight properties, and the files tested here declare neither — they sit at SDK defaults. Applying a guessed blend to a spine correction produces motion that looks plausible but is wrong, which in a review tool is worse than being visibly incomplete. If you need true composited playback, check the intended blend mode with whoever authored the file and it becomes implementable rather than guesswork. Until then, treat a multi-layer file's playback here as the base take.

Rig bones & multiple skeletons in one file

Production rigs carry bones that are part of the skeleton but never deform the mesh — control handles, IK targets, reference roots. They sit wherever the rigger parked them, often metres from the body or back at the origin. Drawn as joints they stretch the marker cloud far outside the mesh, which reads as the markers being offset or rotated from the geometry when nothing is actually misaligned. Measured on a real retarget rig: joints spanning 4.8 m against a 0.57 m mesh.

The Show non-deforming bones toggle controls whether those are drawn. If joints look scattered well beyond the body, that's what you're seeing.

A single FBX can also contain more than one skeleton. A retarget file typically holds both the target rig (which the mesh is skinned to) and the source mocap skeleton, positioned apart in the scene. Skeletons are detected by walking each bone to its top-most bone ancestor — not by name, since names repeat across skeletons in real files — and the one the mesh is skinned to is shown by default so markers and geometry agree.

Mesh display — textured, shaded, wireframe

When a file carries mesh geometry (FBX character exports usually do; C3D and BVH never do), a Mesh selector appears in the viewer controls: Textured (as authored, including texture maps), Shaded (flat grey, no textures — better for reading form and silhouette), Wireframe, or Off to show only markers and skeleton. The control stays hidden for files with no mesh rather than offering a dead option.

Skinning limit: GPU skinning here supports 4 bone influences per vertex. Rigs that bind a vertex to more keep the 4 strongest, and the kept weights are renormalised. That redistributes a small amount of influence rather than collapsing geometry — measured on a real 500k-vertex character rig at about 1% of vertices losing ~1.6% of their influence. Where it happens you'll see the exact figures reported on load. The effect is localised to areas of heavy bone overlap (shoulders, hips, cloth); joint positions and the skeleton are unaffected.

Meshes render double-sided. The data-space to render-space conversion involves an axis swap, which reverses triangle winding — without double-siding, surfaces would render inside-out.

Captury BVH / C3D / CSV support
  • Not based on an external published convention — Captury's file formats and joint-naming conventions were reverse-engineered and cross-validated directly: matching a BVH file's forward-kinematics-solved joint positions against the same session's ambiguous C3D point labels, for two different marker-count configurations.
  • Specific validation numbers are documented directly in the code (e.g. "65 of 86 points matched to within 0.0mm").

Participants & sessions

Participants & saved sessions

The Participant panel (name, height, weight, BMI) appears on each biomechanics protocol tab and is the same shared record — edit it in one and the others update immediately. Height feeds the cross-check in each report and the bike fit calculations; bike measurements live on the Bike Fit tab only, since nothing else uses them.

Save Session (top right) records the current tab's results against a session name you give it, with the timestamp captured automatically. Participants are optional and can be several names — where a file contains more than one person, the field is pre-filled from whoever File Review detected.

Sessions (top right) lists everything saved. It's stored in this browser only and never uploaded. Summaries and reference photos are kept, but not the original capture file — raw takes run well past what a browser can store — so the filename is recorded as a reminder of what to reload.
